Research note · August 2026

Forty Years of Trying to Make Codebases Interpretable

Every major attempt to help humans understand large codebases — what got adopted, what died, and the recurring reasons why. Outcomes for the non-obvious cases (Sourcetrail, CodeSee, Sourcegraph, bloop, stack graphs, DeepWiki) verified against primary sources, linked in each card.

Durable success Alive, niche Survived by pivoting Dead / abandoned

Era 1 · 1984–2000

Prose and generated docs

The founding argument: programs should be explained to humans. The founding failure: asking humans to maintain the explanation.

Literate programming Failed, then mutated 1984

Knuth's WEB: write the program as an essay, extract compilable code mechanically. Nobody wanted to maintain two representations of one program, and the essay drifted from the code. But the diagnosis was right — the idea won decades later in a narrower form, where the prose is the deliverable:

Jupyter notebooks: literate programming's commercially successful descendant — for analysis narratives, not codebases. jupyter.org

Javadoc & Doxygen Durable success 1995 / 1997

Doxygen output generated from a C++ class. Wikimedia Commons

What worked: inverted the effort — derive the document from the code instead of writing about it. Zero marginal cost, can't go stale. Still the most durable lesson in the field.

What didn't: generated reference is a phone book, not a map. "Why does this module exist and who calls it" is still unanswered by doc generators, forty years in.

Era 2 · 1990s–2000s

Diagrams as blueprints: the UML/CASE wave

A UML CASE tool of the era (Umbrello, KDE). Rational Rose looked much the same. Wikimedia Commons

Rational Rose & round-trip engineering Boom, then collapse 1990s–2003

Briefly a genuine commercial triumph — IBM paid $2.1B for Rational in 2003. The pitch: model the system visually, generate code from the model, sync changes both ways ("round-trip engineering").

What killed it: round-trip never actually worked. The model and the code diverged immediately, and maintaining the model became a second job producing no runtime value. Agile positioned itself explicitly against this ("working software over comprehensive documentation") and won. Sparx Enterprise Architect survives where a model is a compliance artifact.

The lesson, twice-underlined by later eras: any interpretability artifact whose freshness depends on human discipline is stale within weeks — and a stale map is worse than no map.

Era 3 · 2000s–present

Search and navigation: the success column

Most of the genuine wins live here. The common thread: used hundreds of times a day, inside an existing workflow, artifact derived automatically from source.

Language Server Protocol Industry-wide success 2016–

Find-references in VS Code, powered by LSP. VS Code docs

What worked: solved the M×N languages-times-editors problem with a protocol, subsidized by a platform owner (Microsoft). Go-to-definition and hover docs for every language in every editor. The single biggest win in the entire space.

Sourcegraph The commercial success 2013–

Sourcegraph code search. sourcegraph.com

What worked: ~$10M revenue and 800K users by 2021; Uber, Stripe, Dropbox, Plaid. Note what was sellable: not "understanding" as such but daily-workflow search across thousands of repos plus batch changes — pain that only exists at enterprise scale, sold to enterprises.

What didn't: the prosumer tiers. Cody free/pro discontinued July 2025; the Amp agent spun off Dec 2025; code search re-aimed at feeding context to AI agents.

GitHub stack graphs Archived 2025 2021–2025

Name resolution as graph paths. GitHub blog, 2021

What worked: zero-config precise go-to-definition on github.com, technically elegant, shipped for Python and TypeScript.

What didn't: per-language grammar work was expensive and never scaled past a few languages; the repo was archived September 2025 as LLM approaches made the precision-per-effort tradeoff look bad.

grep, ctags, OpenGrok, Google Code Search, Kythe Mixed 1980s–

ctags/cscope/grep: primitive, zero-config, in the editor — still used daily after 40 years.

OpenGrok (Sun, 2005): self-hosted code search, quietly adopted inside many large companies. Real OSS success, never a business.

Google's internal Code Search: the tool ex-Googlers consistently miss most — proof the value is enormous when it's free, fast, and universal. The public version still shut down in 2012: valuable internally ≠ product externally.

Kythe (2015): Google's universal indexing schema, open-sourced, influential (LSIF and SCIP descend from it) — and too heavy for almost anyone else to deploy.

Era 4 · 2007–2024

Visualization: the graveyard

The most-loved and least-survivable category. Two independent post-mortems name the same two killers: occasional use can't sustain subscriptions, and multi-language parsing is a treadmill.

CodeCity Never left academia ~2007

A codebase as a city: buildings are classes, height is methods, districts are packages. Richard Wettel

What worked: striking demos, dozens of papers, a whole "software cartography" research wave.

What didn't: nobody returned to the city after the first visit. Zero adopted tools came out of the entire academic wave.

Sourcetrail Abandoned 2021 2016–2021

Interactive call/dependency graphs linked to source. CoatiSoftware/Sourcetrail

What worked: users genuinely loved it — the shutdown HN thread is full of grief.

What didn't: failed commercially, went open source 2019, abandoned 2021. The maintainers cite the LLVM/JDK multi-platform parsing treadmill; an HN commenter names the deeper problem — "call graph visualizers are the sort of thing you need only once or every once in a while… very difficult to monetize."

CodeSee Shut down Feb 2024 2019–2024

Auto-generated, always-current codebase maps — a direct attempt to fix UML's staleness problem. Archived from codesee.io, 2023.

What worked: raised VC, thousands of free users, doubled customer logos in 2023. The maps really did stay current.

What didn't: the founder's post-mortem: sales growth was inconsistent, and covering "more complex codebases, more IDEs, more tech stacks, and more programming languages… would have taken time that we didn't have." Assets acquired by GitKraken. Same two killers as Sourcetrail, named independently.

Era 5 · 1996–present

Architecture analysis: the durable niche

Generic "understand your architecture" is a vitamin. Every survivor here found a painkiller framing: compliance, security, or staffing risk.

SciTools Understand 30 profitable years 1996–

Call "butterfly" graph in Understand. scitools.com

What worked: never famous, never died — sold for three decades to aerospace, defense, automotive, embedded: buyers with certification requirements and million-line C codebases. Interpretability sells when it's attached to a compliance or safety budget. Structure101, Lattix, and NDepend survive in adjacent niches: architects buy them, developers don't.

CodeScene Modest real traction 2015–

Hotspots: circle size = code volume, red = frequently-changed complexity. codescene.com

The interesting move: mines git history rather than the code — hotspots, knowledge maps, bus-factor risk, change coupling. The repo's history is an interpretability signal the code itself can't provide, and "which engineer leaving would strand this code" is a question managers pay for.

Related: CodeQL (Semmle → GitHub, 2019) began partly as a comprehension tool — "query your code like a database" — and won by narrowing to security, where a query result has a dollar value.

Era 6 · 2019–present

Docs that can't go stale, and the AI wave

DeepWiki The biggest adoption yet — as a loss leader 2025–

Auto-generated wiki for microsoft/vscode: architecture overview, diagrams, Q&A. Cognition, April 2025

What worked: URL-swap UX (github.com → deepwiki.com), LLM generation sidesteps the per-language parsing treadmill that killed Sourcetrail and CodeSee. By late 2025: 1.4M repos indexed, 20M+ queries served — the closest thing yet to a successful general-purpose codebase-interpretability product.

The caveat: it's free, it exists as marketing and infrastructure for Devin — and it was originally built so the agent could understand codebases. Human usefulness was a discovered side effect.

"Chat with your codebase" startups Feature-not-product 2023–

bloop, Adrenaline, Onboard AI, early Greptile: almost all dead or pivoted. bloop's founders are explicit: "most users preferred to use other products like Cursor and GitHub Copilot which had bundled much of the same functionality."

Codebase Q&A collapsed from a product into a feature of the IDE or agent you already pay for. bloop pivoted to COBOL→Java migration (real enterprise budgets), then Vibe Kanban; Greptile pivoted to AI code review and is doing well there.

Swimm & Mintlify The wedge wasn't the business 2019–

Swimm: docs coupled to code ranges, CI breaks when the referenced code changes — the most serious attack on doc-drift. Raised ~$33M; adoption stayed modest (writing docs is still work, even drift-protected). Repositioned toward legacy/mainframe code understanding, where documentation gaps are existential.

Mintlify: started as an AI docstring writer — an interpretability tool — and found the real business in docs hosting. The comprehension feature was the wedge, not the product.

Synthesis

The pattern, compressed

What worked

  • Derived, never hand-maintained. Every survivor generates its artifact from source (Doxygen, LSP, Sourcegraph, DeepWiki). Every hand-fed artifact rotted (UML, wikis, literate programs).
  • Daily-frequency embedding. Search and navigation are used constantly, so they sustained products and standards. Understanding-as-a-destination gets visited twice: at onboarding, then never.
  • A buyer with a named pain. Enterprise multi-repo scale (Sourcegraph), safety certification (Understand), security (CodeQL), COBOL cliffs (bloop, Swimm 2.0). "Your team will understand the code better" has never closed a deal by itself.
  • Platform subsidy. The best free infrastructure is monetized elsewhere: LSP (Microsoft), code nav and tree-sitter (GitHub), DeepWiki (Cognition/Devin).

What killed the failures

  • The occasional-use trap. Sourcetrail and CodeSee both had users who loved them, and both died of churn after onboarding week.
  • The language-coverage treadmill. Precise multi-language analysis costs linearly in languages and platforms; small teams drown. LLMs sidestep this — exactly why DeepWiki covers 1.4M repos and stack graphs got archived.
  • Feature-not-product gravity. When a capability gets cheap, the IDE/platform absorbs it — find-references, code maps, chat-with-repo — stranding standalone vendors.
  • Diagram romanticism. People consistently believe they want architecture diagrams; four decades of evidence shows they don't return to them. What people reuse: search, jump-to-definition, and now targeted Q&A.

The open question in 2026

The consumer of codebase interpretability is shifting from humans to agents. DeepWiki was built for Devin before it was a website for humans; Sourcegraph now sells "context for agents"; SCIP and MCP feed indexes into models. Whether human-facing interpretability becomes a mostly-free byproduct of agent infrastructure — the way navigation became a free byproduct of platforms — is the thing to watch.
